title: Who should pay for climate adaptation?

turns.speaker: Lukas
turns.text: The adaptation fund was agreed three years ago and about a tenth of the promised money has actually appeared.

turns.speaker: Nkechi
turns.text: Which is roughly the record of every climate finance pledge. The announcement is the deliverable.

turns.speaker: Bess
turns.text: And a lot of what does arrive is counted twice. Existing aid relabelled, or loans presented as contributions.

turns.speaker: Lukas
turns.text: Loans are the part I find hardest to defend. You're lending a country money to cope with a problem you caused.

turns.speaker: Nkechi
turns.text: Which then shows up in its debt figures and raises its borrowing cost, so it pays twice.

turns.speaker: Bess
turns.text: The counter-argument is capacity rather than willingness. Money moves slowly because there aren't enough prepared projects.

turns.speaker: Nkechi
turns.text: That's partly true and it's also circular. You don't build capacity without predictable funding.

turns.speaker: Lukas
turns.text: The historical responsibility calculation is fairly stark, mind you. Cumulative emissions concentrate in very few countries.

turns.speaker: Bess
turns.text: Though emitting now is a different set of countries, which is what makes the negotiation impossible.

turns.speaker: Nkechi
turns.text: Adaptation is the cheapest part of all of it, though. Early warning systems cost almost nothing and save enormous numbers of lives.

turns.speaker: Lukas
turns.text: Why is it the least funded, then?

turns.speaker: Nkechi
turns.text: Because mitigation has a market and adaptation doesn't. Nobody sells a sea wall to a shareholder.

turns.speaker: Bess
turns.text: Which is an argument for public money doing what markets won't.

points: About a tenth of the promised adaptation fund has materialised three years after agreement.
Bess notes much of what arrives is double-counted relabelled aid or loans presented as contributions.
Nkechi argues loans make affected countries pay twice, through repayment and higher borrowing costs.
The capacity argument for slow disbursement is partly true but circular, since capacity requires predictable funding.
Historical responsibility concentrates in few countries while current emissions come from others, complicating negotiation.
Adaptation is cheap and effective, particularly early warning systems, but least funded because mitigation has a market and adaptation does not.
